newsitem.title: UK: Lloyd's to let market decide on capital structure.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's to let market decide on capital structure.

text.p: The Council of Lloyd's on Monday said it intended to allow market forces to determine its future capital structure despite a report that a move to continuous capital could save 300 million pounds ($506.9 million) annually for th insurers' market.
In so doing it avoided throwing its support behind either side in the ongoing debate over whether its future lies with corporate capital or Names - the traditional backers of the market.
The Council's decision will disappoint many hoping for a more definitive statement after a series of working party reports on its future.

However, it was consistent with comments made at the annual meeting in June where outgoing chairman Sir David Rowland promised there was no hidden agenda to oust Names or do away with the annual venture where syndicates are formed anew each year.
Many managing agents believe that system to be out-dated and expensive and the co-existence of Names and corporate capital unnecessarily complex.
One senior Lloyd's figure has even gone so far as to call it an "anachronistic absurdity".
Corporate capital, first introduced in 1994 now accounts for 44 percent of the market's capital and Rowland predicted it was likely to exceed 50 percent next year.
While the Council of Lloyd's acknowledged there were significant economic benefits to be gained from continuous syndicates, it said it was up to the market to determine how the capital base evolved.
There would, said Rowland, be no move to withdraw the rights of individual Names to continue to trade within the annual venture structure.
Nor would the Council seek to impose its commercial judgement on agents or Names as to the merits of converting to continuous capital, he said.
Instead, its efforts would be focused on providing a level playing field, a free and efficient market place and ensuring Lloyd's distinctive characteristics were not lost.

Critics of the present set up gained some support with the publication of the Syndicate Structure Working Party (SSWP) report, one of a number set up in January to look at the future of Lloyd's after the near disastrous losses of the late 1980s and early 1990s.
It concluded there would be clear benefits in moving toward a permanent capital structure at Lloyd's and that the annual venture put it at a disadvantage to other insurance businesses.
Greater investment in business development, support for new products, greater freedom to underwrite multi-year risks and costs were all identified as advantages of continuous syndicates.

The report said a 180 million pound increase in investment returns from matching syndicate assets to liabilities, 65 million pounds of cost savings and 55 million pounds savings in members' agents and Lloyd's advisers' fees and profit commission were among the benefits of a move to continuous capital.

It backed the acquisition of syndicate members' capacity rights by managing agents as the best means of transition, prompting the Lloyd's regulatory Board to produce a consultation document on bilateral deals.
Lloyd's said it would be looking at ways to improve available conversion routes for Names, would seek to improve the annual venture and devise new structures to attract private capital.

Lloyd's also elaborated the guiding principles for future development of the market first set out at the annual meeting in June and backed the findings of another report by the capacity working group that it was not appropriate to introduce mechanisms to plan and manage capacity centrally. ($ = 0.591 British Pounds)
